paragraphs: Kol dabar sheasur leyisrael laasoto, asur lomar lenakeri laasoto; velo od ella apillu shello amar lo hayyisrael laasot, ella hannakeri meelayv umeatzmo asa melaka letzorek yisrael, asur lehanot mimmenna beshabbat, ella tzarik lehamtin laereb bikde sheyyeasu.

clarification.explanation: Anything a Jew is forbidden to do himself on the Sabbath is also forbidden to tell a gentile to do in his place. And not only that — even if the Jew did not ask the gentile at all to do anything, but the gentile did so on his own initiative for the Jew's benefit, the Jew is forbidden to benefit from that labor on the Sabbath itself, but must wait until evening (the Sabbath's conclusion) to benefit from it.
takeaways: It is forbidden to tell a gentile to do on the Sabbath something a Jew is forbidden to do himself.
Even if the gentile did it on his own initiative, without being asked, it is forbidden to benefit from it on the Sabbath itself — one must wait until the Sabbath's conclusion.

paragraphs: "p sheasur lehannicha lenakeri laasot melaka leyisrael beshabbat - ben bechinnam, ben besakar, dehaynu sekir yom - v"p sheoseh hannakeri meatzmo velo amar lo hayyisrael laasot lo beshabbat, mikkol maqom im hannakeri oseh betorat qabbelanut, sheqqibbel alayv laasot kak vekak - ben sheoseh bishbil yisrael mishshello, ben sheoseh bishbil yisrael mishshel yisrael, dehaynu shennatan lo beged litpor veqatzatz lo sakar bead kol habbeged - hare zeh muttar lehannicho laasot hammelaka beshabbat; ubilbad shello yomar lo "aseh beshabbat!" veken muttar litten lo habbeged beereb-shabbat samuk lachasheka, "p sheyyodea bevadday sheyyaaseh hannakeri beshabbat, v"p shehayyisrael chapetz bekak belibbo, yaan ki hannakeri addata denapsheh qaabed letobat atzmo kede leqabbel sekaro, veen hayisrael omer lo beperush sheyyaaseh beshabbat; beram tzarik lizzaher shello yaaseh hammelaka bebet yisrael mippene marit haayin, sheen yodeim haolam shehu qabbelan. venimtza shelosha tenaim baddabar: haechad, sheqqatzatz sekaro; vehashsheni, shello yomar lo laasot beshabbat; vehashshelishi, deeno oseh bebet yisrael.

Bammeh debarim amurim? beqabbelan sheoseh melaka bedabar hattalush sheyyukal laasotah hannakeri bebeto, delekka chashash marit haayin, abal im oseh hammelaka bimchubbar, kegon libnot beto shel yisrael o liqtzor sadehu vekayyotze bazeh, asur apillu beqabbelan, kevan degaluy leolam shezzo hammelaka shel yisrael - choshebin shehannakeri hu sekir-yom veeno qabbelan. vaapillu meleket hattalush, im hi mepursemet vidua larabbim shehi shel yisrael, venaaset bemaqom galuy umepursam, kegon sepina shedderek laasotah al sepat hannahar vekayyotze bazeh, asur mippene marit haayin. vekol melaka sheoseh hannakeri beqabbelanut bebeto - im enah yedua larabbim shehi shel yisrael, "p sheyyodeim bah qetzat bene-adam, lo gazeru bah rabbanan.

clarification.explanation: Even though it is forbidden to have a gentile perform labor for a Jew on the Sabbath (whether for free or for daily wages), and even when the gentile does so on his own without the Jew asking him — nevertheless if the gentile works as a "contractor" (that is, he has undertaken to complete a specific piece of work in full, whether with his own materials or the Jew's materials, for a fixed price agreed in advance — for example, he received a garment to sew for a fixed sum) — it is permitted to let him do the work on the Sabbath, provided the Jew does not explicitly tell him "do it on the Sabbath!" It is also permitted to give him the material on the Sabbath eve close to nightfall, even when it is known for certain that the gentile will work on the Sabbath, since the gentile is working for his own benefit in order to receive his payment, and the Jew did not instruct him to do it specifically on the Sabbath. Nevertheless, one must be careful that the gentile not perform the work inside the Jew's house, so that it does not appear as though he is a daily employee rather than a contractor (appearance of impropriety). There are three necessary conditions here: (a) that the price is fixed in advance, (b) that he was not told to do it specifically on the Sabbath, (c) that he not work in the Jew's house. All this applies only to contracting on a detached object that can be made in the gentile's own house, where there is no concern of appearance of impropriety; but if the work is performed on something attached to the ground (such as building the Jew's house or harvesting his field), it is forbidden even as contracting, since to all appearances it looks like the work of a daily employee. Likewise, work on a detached object that is well known and publicized to belong to a Jew and is done in a public place (such as a boat being built on a riverbank) is forbidden due to appearance of impropriety. But contracted work done in the gentile's house, not known publicly to belong to a Jew, was not subject to this decree by the Sages, even if some people know about it to some extent.
takeaways: It is permitted to employ a gentile as a contractor (work for a price fixed in advance, not a daily wage) on the Sabbath, as long as he was not told to do it specifically on the Sabbath and he does not work in the Jew's house.

Contracting is permitted only for a detached object with no concern of appearance of impropriety; work on something attached to the ground (such as construction) or in a place visible to the public is forbidden even as contracting.

paragraphs: Reuben bana beto venishar lo tel apar barechob lipne bepetach beto, veshekar haggoy beqabbelanut sheyyipneh heapar kullo besakar qatzub, vehaggoy ba lepannot heapar beshabbat; en tzarik limchot beyado "p shehakkol yodeim shezzeh heapar hu shel yisrael, im kol zeh hakkol yodeim sheen darkam lepannot apar kazeh biskirut yom ella beqabbelanut; vekaasher heela harab "nedib-leb", cheleq ', orach chayyim, siman y'. upoh irenu y" gam ken yadua ubarur etzel hakkol deen osim zeh ella beqabbelanut, veshari.

clarification.explanation: A practical case: a person built his house and was left with a mound of earth in the street before his doorway, and he hired a gentile as a contractor to clear away all the earth for a fixed price, and the gentile came to clear the earth on the Sabbath. In such a case there is no need to protest, even though everyone knows the earth belongs to the Jew, since everyone also knows that the world's way is to clear away such earth only through contracting and not through daily wages, and therefore there is no concern of appearance of impropriety here. And so too the custom in Baghdad is known and clear to all that work of this kind is done only through contracting, and it is therefore permitted.
takeaways: Clearing away earth by a gentile contractor is permitted, even when it is known the earth belongs to a Jew, since it is known to all that such work is always done through contracting.

paragraphs: "p sheamarnu shemmuttar laasot betalush beqabbelanut im oseq haggoy bebeto, im kol zeh, im zeh hattalush hu letzorek hamchubbar, kegon lipsol abanim uletaqqen qorot, o letaqqen mechitztza vekayyotze, dekol ellu hu mishqaam babbinyan veyihyu bimchubbar - dinam kemo habbinyan atzmo veasur laasotam apillu bebet haggoy veen nikkarim shehem shel yisrael. vetzarik limchot beyad haggoy sheoseq bahem im hu oseh otam betok hattechum; mihu, im asa haggoy beshabbat velo micha beyado, yesh lehattir leshaqqeam aach"k bebinyan, kevan dehaggoy asa bebeto vehaya zeh haeseq beqabbelanut, kevan deyesh mi shemmattir qabbelanut apillu bimchubbar, keday lismok al sebarato bediabad bedabar zeh.

clarification.explanation: Even though we said that it is permitted for a gentile to work as a contractor on a detached object in his own house, nevertheless if the detached object is ultimately intended to be attached to the ground — such as hewing stones or preparing beams to be set into a building, or repairing a partition — their law is the same as the attached building itself, and it is forbidden to make them even in the gentile's house and even if they are not recognizable as belonging to a Jew. One should protest against the gentile engaged in this if he does so within a Jewish area. However, if the gentile has already done this on the Sabbath and no one protested, it is permitted after the fact to set those parts into the building, since the gentile did this in his own house within the framework of contracting, and there is an opinion that permits contracting even for something intended to become attached — and one may rely on this opinion after the fact.
takeaways: A detached object ultimately intended to become attached (such as stones for a building) — forbidden for a gentile to make as a contractor even in his own house, and one should protest against him.
If it was already done after the fact, it is permitted to use it in the building — one may rely on a lenient opinion after the fact.

paragraphs: Nakeri sekir-yom shebbana beshabbat, "p sheyyisrael keshessekaro leyamim hitna immo beperush shello yaaseh beshabbat, umiddato asa haeseq beshabbat - nakon lehachmir shello yadur bo shum yisrael velo yehaneh bo shum yisrael leolam im nakeri asa zot letobat yisrael lemaher lo eseq; abal im lo nitkavven hannakeri ella raq letobat atzmo kede leqabbel sakar, az apillu baal habbayit atzmo shari leh ladur bo velehanot bo, kevan shehu hitna immo shello yaaseh beshabbat, vehannakeri asa letobat atzmo.

clarification.explanation: A gentile daily employee who built on the Sabbath — even though the Jew, when he hired him for a set period, explicitly stipulated that he not work on the Sabbath, and nevertheless the gentile worked on the Sabbath of his own accord — if the gentile did so out of a desire to help and hasten the work for the Jew's benefit, it is proper to be stringent that even the Jew himself not live in this building nor ever benefit from it. But if the gentile did not intend the Jew's benefit at all, but only his own benefit in order to receive his payment — then even the owner himself may live in the building and benefit from it, since he stipulated with him not to work on the Sabbath, and the gentile worked only for his own benefit.
takeaways: If a hired gentile worked on the Sabbath contrary to an explicit condition, but with the intent of helping the Jew, one should be stringent and not benefit from the result at all.
If the gentile worked only for his own benefit (to receive payment), even the owner himself may benefit from the result.

paragraphs: Im haggoy asa melaka deorayeta leatzmo bemidde daakila, asur leyisrael lehanot mimmenna, shemma yomar laggoy laasot lo; veyesh mattirin, disbira lehu la chayeshinan behaki, verauy lachush ledibre haoserim; veraq bimqom metzuvva vetzorek gadol dehaynu sheat haddechaq, en lachush. vekol zeh eno ella bemidde daakila dehechmiru bah tepe, abal bemidi dela akila lo chasheshu. velaken goy shehidliq et hanner leatzmo, muttar leyisrael lehanot mimmennu, vekannizkar besiman r"v; veayyen magen abraham, siman shk"ch vesiman tqy"z v"machatzit-hashsheqel" sham, veayyen tosepet shabbat, seip qatan y'.

clarification.explanation: If a gentile performed a Torah-forbidden labor for his own benefit involving food, a Jew is forbidden to benefit from it, out of concern that he might come to ask the gentile to do it for him. There is a lenient opinion holding that this concern need not apply, but it is proper to be concerned for the stricter opinion, and only for the sake of a commandment or great need (a pressing situation) need one not be concerned. This entire stringency was stated only regarding food, where the authorities were stricter, but regarding non-food matters there was no concern at all. Therefore, a gentile who lit a candle for himself — a Jew is permitted to benefit from the light.
takeaways: Benefiting from a gentile's labor performed for his own sake, involving food, is forbidden (out of concern one might ask him), except for the sake of a commandment or a great pressing need.
For non-food matters, such as a candle a gentile lit for himself, there is no such concern, and one may benefit from it.

paragraphs: Im yesh ner bebet yisrael uba haggoy vehidliq ner acher, muttar lehishtammesh leoro beod ner harishon doleq, abal leachar shekkaba harishon asur lehishtammesh leor ner hashsheni shehidliq haggoy. veken im natan haggoy shemen banner haddoleq, muttar lehishtammesh ad sheyyikleh hashshemen shehaya bo kebar, veaach"k asur, vekannizkar beshulchan aruk, siman r"v, seip d'. umah shekkatab ht"z za"l seip qatan g', dachu debarayv haacharonim za"l, vekannizkar beseper tosepet shabbat v"matteh yeuddeh" v"chemed mosheh" v"maamar mareddekay". vaana abeda bsh"q "rab-pealim" hebeti reayot gemurot lehokicha hepek sebarat ht"z za"l.

clarification.explanation: If there is already a lit candle in a Jew's house, and a gentile comes and lights an additional candle, it is permitted to use the light of the gentile's candle as long as the first candle (the Jew's) is still burning — but once the first candle has gone out, it is forbidden to use the light of the second candle that the gentile lit. Likewise, if the gentile added oil to a candle that was already burning, it is permitted to use the light until the oil that was already in the candle beforehand runs out, and after that it is forbidden.
takeaways: It is permitted to use the light of a candle a gentile lit only as long as a Jew's earlier candle is burning alongside it — once the first has gone out, it is forbidden.

paragraphs: Pat sheapaah goy palter beshabbat limkor laggoyim - millebad deikka chashasha dechashu bemidde daakila shemma yomar hayisrael legoy laasot, hinneh yesh bazeh od chashashot acherot vehu issur muqtzeh, deulay zeh happat lo haya chittim dachazu lekos ben-hashshemashot, ella haya qemach o issa beben-hashshemashot dela chazu midi; umuqtzeh zeh domeh ligrogarot vetzimmuqin deidchinehu beyadayim, veasur gam achar apiyya; v"p sheyyesh mattirim gam bazeh - leinyan halaka en lismok al hammattirim ella bishat haddechaq, sheddar bikpar yechidi shei epshar lishol lo pat miyyisrael chabero, o letzorek metzuvveh kegon seudat mila vechatan, abal belav haki tzarik lehachmir kisbarat haoserin. ubeinyan shetiyyat hqhvv" (qapeh) sheosin haggoyim bachanuyot shellahem beshabbat beir sherubbah goyim deabedi baabur harob shehem goyim - hinneh ledaat mera"n za"l asur, shello hittir bimleket haggoy leatzmo bemidde daakila ella letzorek metzuvveh; veod bazeh name ikka taam demuqtzeh deiddechi beyadayim, ki qodem qaleh lo hayeta reuya laakila kelal; velaken yesh leesor leyisrael shetiyyat qhvv; veen lehattir ella leadam sheyyesh lo keeb harosh vetzarik lah harbeh. vahagam deharab "zera-emet" za"l helitz bead hannohagim lishtot me hqhvv shebbishshelah haggoy ap-al-pi deqodem haqleh enah reuya laakila, mishshum dela dame ligrogarot vetzimmuqim deiddechi beyadayim – mikkol maqom ledidin deqibbalnu sebarat maran za"l disbira lah bemidi daakila gazerinan shemma yomar lo hayisrael laasot lo, veasur kemo shekkatabnu bedin happat - hinneh gam bazeh yesh leesor mittaam zeh. mihu, poh irenu, mikkamma shanim hurgelu kamma anashim lelek beshabbat lachanuyot shel nakerim velishtot me shachor o mashqeh hqhvv" shemmebashshel hannakeri beshabbat; veen anachnu mochim beyadam mikkamma teamim, veraq anachnu mazhirim otam shello yishtu ella davqa min qhvv" shennitbashshela qodem biatam sham, velo mimmah sheyyebashshel hannakeri achar boam, deshemma yarbeh bishbilam. veken baal habbayit sheshsholeach keli im shelucho lehabi lo qhvv" mebushshelet, lo yiqqach ella min hambushshal mikkebar. ubaal-nepesh yarchiq atzmo milleket sham lishtot me shachor - millebad deissur zeh ledaat mera"n za"l, od rauy shello yesheb bemoshab habbatlanim hazzeh bayyom haqqadosh vehannora hazzeh; veyesh lehaarik bedibre musar bedabar zeh. vehinneh poh irenu yimmatze chanut shel goy zeh hambashshel hqhvv", omedet birchob hayyehudim, veqa chazenan bime hachol derob hayyoshebim sham hem yehudim; ubachanut zo tzarik lehazhiram shello yeleku beshabbat, abal bishar chanuyot - addata derubba degoyim qaabed. vehannizhar lebilti leket lekol chanuyot, tabo alayv beraka.

clarification.explanation: Bread baked by a gentile baker on the Sabbath in order to sell to gentiles — beyond the usual concern that a Jew might tell the gentile to bake for him, there is here an additional concern of muktzeh: it is possible that the flour or dough from which the bread was baked was not yet fit for eating at twilight (the onset of the Sabbath), and therefore its law is that of muktzeh set aside deliberately — which remains forbidden even after baking, similar to dried figs and raisins. Some permit this even in such a case, but in practice one should rely on the leniency only in a pressing situation — such as one who lives alone in a village with no one from whom to request Jewish bread, or for the sake of a mitzvah meal such as a circumcision or a wedding; otherwise one should be stringent, following the stricter view. Regarding drinking coffee that gentiles prepare in their shops on the Sabbath (in a city where most residents are gentiles): according to Maran, it is forbidden, since he permitted benefiting from a gentile's labor performed for himself involving food only for the sake of a commandment — and there is also here an additional concern of muktzeh, since before roasting the coffee beans were entirely unfit for eating. Some permitted drinking such coffee, but in practice — since we have accepted Maran's view that with food one is concerned lest people ask the gentile to do it for them — this too should be forbidden. In Baghdad several people were accustomed for years to go to gentile shops on the Sabbath and drink a black beverage or coffee brewed there on the Sabbath, and although they are not protested against for several reasons, they are warned to drink only from coffee brewed before their arrival and not from what is brewed after their arrival (lest more be brewed because of them). One who is scrupulous with himself should keep away from going there altogether — both because of the prohibition itself and because it is not proper to sit in the company of idlers on this holy day. In particular, there is a gentile's shop on the street of the Jews, most of whose weekday patrons are Jews — there one must be especially warned not to go on the Sabbath; in other shops, whose patrons are mostly gentiles, the law is more lenient. Likewise, a homeowner who sends a vessel by his messenger to bring him brewed coffee should take only from what was already brewed beforehand.
takeaways: Bread baked on the Sabbath by a gentile for sale to gentiles is generally forbidden due to muktzeh and the concern of asking a gentile, except in a great pressing situation or for the sake of a mitzvah.

Coffee prepared by a gentile on the Sabbath is forbidden according to Maran, though the local custom is not to protest against those who drink it, provided they drink only coffee prepared before their arrival.

paragraphs: Kol mechubbar shennashar meelayv o nitlash "y nakeri "p shettelasho leatzmo - ben perot viraqot, ben asabim sheenam reuyim lemaakal adam, apillu sapeq nitleshu hayyom - hare ellu asurim leyisrael bo bayyom, ben baakila, ben betiltul; velaereb muttarim miyyad apillu bevadday nitleshu hayyom. vekol zeh benitleshu mealehen o shettelasham haggoy leatzmo, abal telasham letzorek yisrael, tzarik lehamtin laereb bikde sheyyeasu. vesapeq im nitleshu bishbil yisrael, o yadua shennitleshu bishbil yisrael ella sapeq im nitleshu hayyom o qodem, hare ellu asurim, velaereb muttarim bikde sheyyeasu.

clarification.explanation: Anything attached to the ground that fell off on its own, or was plucked by a gentile (even if he plucked it for his own benefit) — whether fruits and vegetables or plants unfit for human consumption, and even if there is doubt whether they were plucked today — are forbidden to a Jew on the Sabbath day itself, both for eating and for handling; but in the evening (at the Sabbath's conclusion) they are permitted immediately, even if it is certain they were plucked that day. All this applies when they fell off on their own or the gentile plucked them for his own benefit; but if the gentile plucked them for the Jew's benefit, one must wait until evening for the amount of time "needed to do it" (the time it would have taken to do this). And if there is doubt whether they were plucked for the Jew's benefit, or it is known they were plucked for his benefit but there is doubt whether they were plucked today or earlier — they are forbidden, and in the evening are permitted after the time "needed to do it."
takeaways: Fruits or plants plucked on the Sabbath, on their own or by a gentile for himself, are forbidden that day but permitted immediately at the Sabbath's conclusion.
If plucked by a gentile for the Jew's benefit, one must wait at the Sabbath's conclusion only for the time "needed to do it."

paragraphs: Dabar sheen bo chashash tzeda umechubbar bo bayyom, ella raq huba michutz lattechum: im hebio hannakeri leatzmo o hebio lenakeri acher o limkor beir sherubbah nakerim, muttar leyisrael apillu bo bayyom; veim hebio hannakeri leyisrael, asur baakila bo bayyom lemi shehuba bishbilo, laereb yamtin bikde sheyyeasu, abal laacherim muttar apillu bo bayyom. vekevan demuttar laacherim bo bayyom, en lo din muqtzeh leoto habba bishbilo, ella yukal letaltelo kevan derauy laakila laacherim.

clarification.explanation: Something with no concern of trapping or plucking on that day, but only brought from outside the Sabbath boundary: if the gentile brought it for himself, or for another gentile, or in order to sell it in a city where most residents are gentiles — it is permitted to a Jew even on that same day. If the gentile brought it specifically for a particular Jew, it is forbidden to eat on that day only to that Jew for whom it was brought (he must wait until evening for the time "needed to do it"), but it is permitted to other Jews even on that same day. And since it is permitted to others on that same day, the object does not have the law of muktzeh even for the one for whom it was brought, and therefore he too may handle it, since it is fit for eating for others.
takeaways: Something brought from outside the boundary for a particular Jew is forbidden for eating only to him on the Sabbath itself (until evening), but is permitted to other Jews even that same day, and may also be handled.

paragraphs: "g shehabba michutz lattechum muttar lemi shello huba bishbilo, mikkol maqom im hebiu lishne bene-adam, asurim lehachalip zeh im zeh; veayyen "eliyya raba" vetosepet shabbat ushear acharonim.

clarification.explanation: Even though something brought from outside the boundary is permitted to one for whom it was not brought, nevertheless if a gentile brought it specifically for two people (each receiving the portion designated for him), they may not exchange portions between themselves — even though each is forbidden from what was brought for him, they may not permit this by way of exchanging with one another.
takeaways: When a gentile brings items from outside the boundary specifically for two people, they may not exchange the portions between themselves.

paragraphs: Ha deameru: goy shehebi leyisrael michutz lattechum asur leoto habba bishbilo, haynu davqa shehebi haggoy doron mishshello leyisrael, degazerinan shemma yomar yisrael laggoy beperush sheyyabi lo; abal im yisrael hayyosheb bemaqom echad shalach leyisrael chabero doron im haggoy, velo yada yisrael hamshalleach shehaggoy yitakkeb badderek, ella chashab sheyyaggia qodem shabbat, venizdammen shennitakkeb vehebi haddoron leyisrael beshabbat michutz lattechum, hare zeh muttar gam leoto yisrael shebba bishbilo. vedabar zeh meporash behilkot yom tob, siman tqm"v, vehebio harab "tosepet-shabbat" behilkot shabbat, siman shk"h, seip qatan k"h, yeuyyan sham. veap al gab drsh"l za"l katab sheddin zeh hu raq lisbarat rabbenu tam - kebar hissigu ht"z, veken daat hammagen abraham dedin zeh lekulle alema, veken katebu haacharonim za"l; abal im hayyisrael natan haddoron legoy beereb shabbat, sheyyeda beberur shello yaggia haggoy ella beshabbat – asur.

clarification.explanation: The rule that something a gentile brought a Jew from outside the boundary is forbidden to the Jew for whom it was brought was stated only when the gentile brought a gift of his own to the Jew, since then there is concern that the Jew might have explicitly told him to bring it. But if one Jew sent a gift to his fellow Jew by means of a gentile, and the sender did not know the gentile would be delayed along the way — rather he thought the messenger would arrive before the Sabbath began — but in fact the gentile was delayed and brought the gift on the Sabbath from outside the boundary, this is permitted even to the Jew for whom the gift was brought, since here the concern does not apply (since it was not known in advance that he would arrive on the Sabbath). However, if the sending Jew already knew clearly in advance that the gentile would not arrive except on the Sabbath, and nevertheless gave him the gift — this is forbidden.
takeaways: A gift a Jew sent to his fellow via a gentile, which was delayed to the Sabbath by mistake without the sender expecting it, is permitted even to the one for whom it was brought.
If the sender knew in advance the gentile would arrive only on the Sabbath and sent it anyway, it is forbidden.

paragraphs: Kol maqom sheameru shetztzarik lehamtin bikde sheyyeasu, im hu dabar habba mittok hattechum, ella sheissuro mechamat tzeda o mechubbar - tzarik lehamtin bikde sheyyeasu mittechillat hallayla; abal hu dabar sheen bo tzeda umechubbar, yesh omerim sheen hallayla oleh min hacheshbon, mishshum deen regilut lehabi ballayla mimmaqom rachoq, vetzarik lehamtin bikde sheyyeasu lemachar beyom rishon. mihu, kevan sheyyatza yom rishon, day; sheim tzarik lo derek y"d shaot, en omerim lehamtin ad shaa shenit min hallayla, ella kevan sheyyatza yom rishon muttar miyyad. veyesh omerim deshiur bikde sheyyeasu meshaarin min hallayla; ubimqom tzorek yesh lismok al hammeqillin; ubeyom tob yesh lismok al hammeqillin bekol gavna. upoh irenu, regilut lehabi ballayla, laken osim hacheshbon min hallayla lekulle alema.

clarification.explanation: Wherever it is said that one must wait "the time needed to do it" (the time it takes to perform the act) — if it concerns something within the Sabbath boundary whose prohibition is only due to trapping or attachment to the ground, one should begin counting the time from the start of the night (the onset of the Sabbath's conclusion). But if it concerns something with no concern of trapping or attachment (such as bringing something from outside the boundary), some say the night is not included in the count, since there is no practice of bringing things from a distant place at night, and therefore one must wait "the time needed to do it" only the following day, Sunday. Nevertheless, once Sunday has begun, this suffices — even if the journey takes fourteen hours, there is no need to wait a second hour from nightfall; rather, the moment Sunday begins, it is immediately permitted. Some say that in this case too one should count from nightfall — and in a case of need one may rely on the lenient opinion, and on a Festival one may rely on the lenient view in any case. In Baghdad, since it was accepted practice to bring things even at night, the time was calculated from the start of the night according to all opinions.
takeaways: The law of "the time needed to do it" — for something within the boundary, count from the start of the night; for something brought from outside the boundary, some say to count only from Sunday, though in a case of need one may be lenient.

paragraphs: Laqat haggoy asabim letzorek behemto - im eno makkiro leyisrael, maakil acharayv beopen zeh: dehaynu sheomed bipne habbehema beinyan shello tukal lintot ella derek sham, deillu lehaamidah alehen asur, dechayeshinan shemma yittol beyado veyaakilenna, vehem muqtzim shennilqetu hayyom; abal im zeh haggoy makkiro leyisrael, asur lehaakil acharayv, gezera shemma yarbeh bishbilo, veken kol kayyotze bazeh deikka lemichash beh shemma yarbeh bishbilo, asur; abal bedabar delet beh hay chashasha, kegon shehidliq haggoy ner leatzmo, o asa kebes leatzmo lered bo, muttar leyisrael lehanot mimmennu apillu im makkiro. veim maasayv mokichin sheasa letzorek yisrael, kegon shehidliq ner bebet yisrael vehalak lo, hare zeh asur lehanot mimmenna; vekol shekken im amar bepiv shelletzorek yisrael hu oseh, deasur.

clarification.explanation: A gentile who gathered plants for his own animal's use — if the gentile does not know the Jew, it is permitted to feed the Jew's animal from these plants only indirectly: by the person standing beside the animal in such a way that it cannot turn and eat except by that means, but it is forbidden to place the animal directly facing the plants, out of concern that one might take them by hand and feed the animal — since they are muktzeh, having been gathered that day. But if the gentile knows the Jew, it is forbidden to feed the animal from the plants at all, out of concern that the gentile might gather more for the Jew's benefit. Anything carrying such a concern that the gentile might do more for the Jew's sake is forbidden. But something with no such concern — such as a gentile lighting a candle for himself, or making a ramp (a step) to descend by — is permitted for a Jew to benefit from even if the gentile knows him. If the gentile's actions demonstrate that he did it for the Jew's benefit (such as lighting a candle in the Jew's house and leaving), it is forbidden to benefit from it; and all the more so if the gentile explicitly said he was doing it for the Jew's benefit — then it is certainly forbidden.
takeaways: Plants gathered by a gentile for his animal — if he does not know the Jew, it is permitted to feed the Jew's animal from them indirectly; if he knows him, it is forbidden out of concern he might gather more for his sake.
Something a gentile clearly did for himself (like lighting a candle) may be benefited from even if he knows the Jew, unless his actions show he did it for the Jew's sake.

paragraphs: Im laqat haggoy asabim meelayv umeatzmo - hen mishshello, hen mishshel hepqer - veheekil lebehemat yisrael, en tzarik hayisrael limchot beyado. v"g deim hidliq meatzmo et hanner letzorek yisrael tzarik limchot beyado, shane hatam deyisrael gupeh neheneh min hanner, mah sheen ken haka shehu hanaat behemto, shari. umihu im ragil bekak, dehaynu sheasa kak shene peamim, tzarik limchot beyado "g shehu hanaat behemto bilbad.

clarification.explanation: If a gentile gathered plants on his own initiative — whether from his own property or ownerless property — and fed them to a Jew's animal, there is no need for the Jew to protest against him. Even though if a gentile lit a candle on his own for the Jew's benefit one must protest against him, the situation there is different since the Jew himself benefits from the candle, which is not the case here where only the animal benefits — and this is therefore permitted. Nevertheless, if the gentile is accustomed to do this regularly (that is, he has already done it twice), one must protest against him, even though the benefit is only to the animal.
takeaways: An animal's benefit from plants a gentile gathered on his own is permitted, with no need to protest — unless the gentile repeats this regularly, in which case one must protest.

paragraphs: Goy shebba littol mashkono shebbeyad yisrael, muttar litteno lo; veraq lo yihyeh hayisrael nose venoten beyado, ella yasim lepanayv vehaggoy yiqqach meatzmo. veim en hayisrael maamin laggoy, asur leyisrael lihyot areb mishshum "mimmetzo cheptzeka" (yeshaya nch, yg), ukemo shekkatab b"tosepet-shabbat" za"l.

clarification.explanation: A gentile who comes on the Sabbath to take back an object that was held by a Jew as a pledge (collateral), it is permitted for the Jew to give him the object — but the Jew is forbidden to hand it directly from hand to hand ("carrying and giving it into his hand"); rather he must place the object before the gentile, and the gentile shall take it himself. And if the Jew does not trust the gentile (fearing he will not repay the debt), the Jew is forbidden to serve as guarantor for him on the Sabbath, due to the prohibition of "seeking your affairs and speaking of matters" (engaging in weekday affairs on the Sabbath).
takeaways: It is permitted to return a pledge to a gentile on the Sabbath, but it must be placed before him, not handed directly from hand to hand.
It is forbidden for a Jew to serve as guarantor for a gentile on the Sabbath, due to the prohibition of "seeking your affairs and speaking of matters."

paragraphs: Mi shellahut achar shetiyyat hattuton, asur lelek etzel haggoy sheshshoteh tuton, veyiptach yisrael et piv viqabbel heashan mippiv, veken kol kayyotze bazeh, vekannizkar bechesed laalapim; veayyen "admat-qodesh", cheleq ', siman d', mah sheheerik beinyan zeh.

clarification.explanation: One who craves tobacco smoking ("tutun") — is forbidden to go to a gentile who is smoking, and open his mouth to receive the smoke from the gentile's mouth, and all similar acts (Chessed LaAlafim; and see "Admat Kodesh," which elaborated on this matter).
takeaways: One who craves smoking — is forbidden to receive tobacco smoke from the mouth of a gentile who is smoking (and all similar acts).
